title: Solving Basic Trigonometric Equations
subject: mathematics

theory.introduction: Basic trigonometric equations are equations that can be transformed into a form involving a single basic trigonometric function such as sin(x), cos(x), or tan(x). The main goal is to find every angle that satisfies the equation. This requires more than simply using an inverse trigonometric function because sine, cosine, and tangent are periodic and can produce the same value at multiple angles.

sections.title: What Is a Basic Trigonometric Equation?

content.text: For sin(x) = a, find the angles where sine has value a and include all required solutions.

Start by isolating the trigonometric function, determine the relevant reference/principal angle, generate every branch, and then express or filter the solutions as requested. The reason these branches repeat comes from periodicity, covered in trig-equations-02; interval filtering is covered in trig-equations-09 and general notation in trig-equations-11.
Many equations are not initially written in the form sin(x) = a, cos(x) = a, or tan(x) = a.
For example, 2sin(x) − 1 = 0 can be rearranged to 2sin(x) = 1 and then sin(x) = 1/2.
The trigonometric solving step should normally begin only after the function has been isolated.
For an equation of the form sin(x) = a, first check that −1 ≤ a ≤ 1.
Use sin⁻¹(a) to obtain a principal angle or use the unit circle to identify the corresponding reference angle.
Sine is positive in Quadrants I and II and negative in Quadrants III and IV.
Therefore, for most values strictly between −1 and 1, two solutions occur during one complete revolution.
For all real solutions, periodicity must be included.
The reference angle is the positive acute angle between the terminal side of an angle and the x-axis.
If the reference angle is α and sine is positive, the solutions in one revolution occur in Quadrants I and II.
These angles are α and π − α.
If sine is negative, the solutions occur in Quadrants III and IV. The corresponding angles in 0 ≤ x < 2π can be written as π + α and 2π − α.
For cos(x) = a, use the unit circle and symmetry to locate the angles.
For tan(x) = a, find the reference angle and use tangent's period of π.

formulas.name: General Sine Solution
formulas.expression: sin(x) = a  ⇒  x = (−1)ⁿ sin⁻¹(a) + nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Represents all real solutions when −1 ≤ a ≤ 1. This compact formula automatically accounts for the two sine solution families and the 2π periodicity.

formulas.name: Two-Form Sine Solution
formulas.expression: sin(x) = a  ⇒  x = sin⁻¹(a) + 2nπ  or  x = π − sin⁻¹(a) + 2nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Shows the two repeating solution families explicitly. It is often easier for students to understand than the compact (−1)ⁿ form.

formulas.name: Sine Equals Sine
formulas.expression: sin(x) = sin(θ)  ⇒  x = θ + 2nπ  or  x = π − θ + 2nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Use this when both sides are sine functions. The two families come from the symmetry of sine within one complete revolution.

formulas.name: General Cosine Solution
formulas.expression: cos(x) = a  ⇒  x = ±cos⁻¹(a) + 2nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Represents all real solutions when −1 ≤ a ≤ 1. The ± accounts for the two cosine solution families.

formulas.name: Two-Form Cosine Solution
formulas.expression: cos(x) = a  ⇒  x = cos⁻¹(a) + 2nπ  or  x = 2π − cos⁻¹(a) + 2nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Shows the two repeating cosine solution families explicitly for a principal angle in the standard first-cycle range.

formulas.name: Cosine Equals Cosine
formulas.expression: cos(x) = cos(θ)  ⇒  x = 2nπ ± θ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Use this when both sides are cosine functions. The two families arise because cosine is an even function and has period 2π.

formulas.name: General Tangent Solution
formulas.expression: tan(x) = a  ⇒  x = tan⁻¹(a) + nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Represents all real solutions. Tangent has period π, so only one solution family is required.

formulas.name: Tangent Equals Tangent
formulas.expression: tan(x) = tan(θ)  ⇒  x = θ + nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Use this when both sides are tangent functions. The solutions repeat every π because tangent has period π.

formulas.name: Sine Equals Zero
formulas.expression: sin(x) = 0  ⇒  x = nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Sine is zero on the x-axis of the unit circle, at every integer multiple of π.

formulas.name: Cosine Equals Zero
formulas.expression: cos(x) = 0  ⇒  x = π/2 + nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Cosine is zero on the y-axis of the unit circle, at odd multiples of π/2.

formulas.name: Tangent Equals Zero
formulas.expression: tan(x) = 0  ⇒  x = nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Tangent is zero whenever sine is zero and cosine is nonzero.

formulas.name: Sine Positive Quadrants
formulas.expression: sin(x) > 0  in Quadrants I and II
formulas.explanation: The y-coordinate of the unit-circle point is positive in Quadrants I and II.

formulas.name: Sine Negative Quadrants
formulas.expression: sin(x) < 0  in Quadrants III and IV
formulas.explanation: The y-coordinate of the unit-circle point is negative in Quadrants III and IV.

formulas.name: Cosine Positive Quadrants
formulas.expression: cos(x) > 0  in Quadrants I and IV
formulas.explanation: The x-coordinate of the unit-circle point is positive in Quadrants I and IV.

formulas.name: Cosine Negative Quadrants
formulas.expression: cos(x) < 0  in Quadrants II and III
formulas.explanation: The x-coordinate of the unit-circle point is negative in Quadrants II and III.

formulas.name: Tangent Positive Quadrants
formulas.expression: tan(x) > 0  in Quadrants I and III
formulas.explanation: Tangent is sin(x)/cos(x), so it is positive when sine and cosine have the same sign.

formulas.name: Tangent Negative Quadrants
formulas.expression: tan(x) < 0  in Quadrants II and IV
formulas.explanation: Tangent is sin(x)/cos(x), so it is negative when sine and cosine have opposite signs.

formulas.name: Sine Range
formulas.explanation: An equation sin(x) = a has no real solution when a < −1 or a > 1.

formulas.name: Cosine Range
formulas.explanation: An equation cos(x) = a has no real solution when a < −1 or a > 1.

formulas.name: Tangent Range
formulas.expression: tan(x) ∈ ℝ
formulas.explanation: Tangent can take every real value, although it is undefined at x = π/2 + nπ.

formulas.name: Sine Period
formulas.expression: sin(x + 2π) = sin(x)
formulas.explanation: Sine repeats every 2π radians or 360°.

formulas.name: Cosine Period
formulas.expression: cos(x + 2π) = cos(x)
formulas.explanation: Cosine repeats every 2π radians or 360°.

formulas.name: Tangent Period
formulas.expression: tan(x + π) = tan(x)
formulas.explanation: Tangent repeats every π radians or 180°.

formulas.name: Degree-Radian Conversion
formulas.expression: 180° = π radians,  360° = 2π radians
formulas.explanation: Use these relationships when converting between degree and radian forms.

formulas.name: Tangent Domain Restriction
formulas.expression: x ≠ π/2 + nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Tangent is undefined wherever cosine is zero.

examples.question: Solve sin(x) = 1/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/6 because sin(π/6) = 1/2. Sine is positive in Quadrants I and II. Therefore x = π/6 and x = π − π/6 = 5π/6.

examples.question: Solve sin(x) = 1/2 for all real x.
examples.solution: The principal angle is π/6 and the second angle is 5π/6. Therefore x = π/6 + 2nπ or x = 5π/6 + 2nπ, where n ∈ ℤ. Equivalently, x = (−1)ⁿπ/6 + nπ.

examples.question: Solve sin(x) = sin(π/6) for all real x.
examples.solution: Using sin(x) = sin(θ), x = θ + 2nπ or x = π − θ + 2nπ. Therefore x = π/6 + 2nπ or x = 5π/6 + 2nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Solve sin(x) = −1/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/6. Sine is negative in Quadrants III and IV. Therefore x = π + π/6 = 7π/6 and x = 2π − π/6 = 11π/6.

examples.question: Solve sin(x) = 0 for all real x.
examples.solution: Sine is zero whenever the terminal side lies on the x-axis. Therefore x = nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Solve sin(x) = 1 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Sine reaches 1 at x = π/2. Therefore the only solution in the half-open interval is x = π/2.

examples.question: Solve sin(x) = 3 for real x.
examples.solution: There is no real solution because sine can only take values from −1 to 1.

examples.question: Solve cos(x) = −√2/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/4 because cos(π/4) = √2/2. Cosine is negative in Quadrants II and III. Therefore x = 3π/4 and x = 5π/4.

examples.question: Solve cos(x) = −1/2 for all real x.
examples.solution: The principal inverse-cosine angle is 2π/3. Using x = ±cos⁻¹(a) + 2nπ gives x = ±2π/3 + 2nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Solve cos(x) = cos(π/3) for all real x.
examples.solution: Use cos(x) = cos(θ) ⇒ x = 2nπ ± θ. Therefore x = 2nπ ± π/3, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Solve cos(x) = 1/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/3. Cosine is positive in Quadrants I and IV. Therefore x = π/3 and x = 5π/3.

examples.question: Solve cos(x) = 0 for all real x.
examples.solution: Cosine is zero at odd multiples of π/2. Therefore x = π/2 + nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Solve cos(x) = −2 for real x.
examples.solution: There is no real solution because cosine can only take values from −1 to 1.

examples.question: Solve tan(x) = √3 for all real x.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/3 because tan(π/3) = √3. Tangent is positive in Quadrants I and III and repeats every π. Therefore x = π/3 + nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Solve tan(x) = −1 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/4. Tangent is negative in Quadrants II and IV. Therefore x = 3π/4 and x = 7π/4.

examples.question: Solve tan(x) = tan(π/4) for all real x.
examples.solution: Using tan(x) = tan(θ) ⇒ x = θ + nπ, we obtain x = π/4 + nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Solve tan(x) = 0 for all real x.
examples.solution: Tangent is zero whenever sine is zero and cosine is nonzero. Therefore x = nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Can x = π/2 be a solution of tan(x) = 1?
examples.solution: No. tan(π/2) is undefined because cos(π/2) = 0. Therefore π/2 is not in the domain of tangent.

examples.question: Solve 2sin(x) − 1 = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: First isolate sine: 2sin(x) = 1, so sin(x) = 1/2. The solutions are x = π/6 and x = 5π/6.

examples.question: Solve 3cos(x) + 2 = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: First isolate cosine: 3cos(x) = −2, so cos(x) = −2/3. Since cosine is negative in Quadrants II and III, use the reference angle cos⁻¹(2/3) and place the solutions in those quadrants.

examples.question: Solve 2tan(x) − 2 = 0 for all real x.
examples.solution: First isolate tangent: 2tan(x) = 2, so tan(x) = 1. Since tan⁻¹(1) = π/4 and tangent has period π, x = π/4 + nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Solve sin(x) = 1/2 for 0° ≤ x < 360°.
examples.solution: The reference angle is 30°. Sine is positive in Quadrants I and II, so x = 30° and x = 150°.

examples.question: Solve cos(x) = −√3/2 for 0° ≤ x < 360°.
examples.solution: The reference angle is 30°. Cosine is negative in Quadrants II and III, so x = 150° and x = 210°.

examples.question: Solve tan(x) = 1 for all real x in degrees.
examples.solution: The reference angle is 45°. Tangent has period 180°, so x = 45° + 180°n, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: What is the basic idea behind solving sin(2x) = 1/2?
examples.solution: Treat 2x as the angle first. The sine equation  sin(2x) = 1/2 has multiple possible values of 2x. After finding those values, divide the resulting equations by 2 to obtain x. The exact number of solutions depends on the interval.

examples.question: Which is usually easier for solving cos(x) = cos(π/3): the unit circle or the cosine-equals-cosine formula?
examples.solution: Both methods work. The direct formula cos(x) = cos(θ) ⇒ x = 2nπ ± θ is especially efficient here because θ is already known.

key_ideas: The first step is usually to isolate the trigonometric function.
The three fundamental basic forms are sin(x) = a, cos(x) = a, and tan(x) = a.
Inverse trigonometric functions provide principal angles, not automatically every solution.
The unit circle provides the exact locations of common trigonometric values.
Reference angles help locate solutions in all four quadrants.
Sine is positive in Quadrants I and II and negative in III and IV.
Cosine is positive in Quadrants I and IV and negative in II and III.
Tangent is positive in Quadrants I and III and negative in II and IV.
Sine and cosine have period 2π.
Tangent has period π.
For sin(x) = sin(θ), use x = θ + 2nπ or x = π − θ + 2nπ.
For cos(x) = cos(θ), use x = 2nπ ± θ.
For tan(x) = tan(θ), use x = θ + nπ.
For sin(x) = a, the compact general solution is x = (−1)ⁿsin⁻¹(a) + nπ.
For cos(x) = a, the general solution is x = ±cos⁻¹(a) + 2nπ.
For tan(x) = a, the general solution is x = tan⁻¹(a) + nπ.
Sine and cosine cannot equal values outside the interval [−1, 1].
Tangent can equal any real number but is undefined at π/2 + nπ.
Restricted intervals require filtering the general solution to the requested range.
General solutions use n ∈ ℤ to represent infinitely many solutions.
Exact unit-circle values should be preferred over decimal approximations when possible.
Degrees and radians must be kept consistent throughout the solution.
The interval endpoints must be checked carefully.
Every final solution should satisfy the original equation.
Recognizing the equation's form helps determine the fastest solving method.
Equations comparing the same trigonometric function on both sides have useful direct general-solution formulas.
Multiple-angle equations use the same basic principles but require additional interval and solution-count care.
misconceptions: Giving only the calculator's inverse-trigonometric answer.
Thinking sin⁻¹(a) means 1/sin(a).
Forgetting that inverse trigonometric functions return principal values.
Forgetting the second solution for sine.
Forgetting the second solution for cosine.
Using the wrong period for tangent.
Assuming tangent has period 2π instead of π.
Using the same quadrant rules for all three functions.
Thinking sine and cosine can take values greater than 1 or less than −1.
Forgetting to isolate the trigonometric function before solving.
Forgetting to include all integer values of n in a general solution.
Treating n as a real number instead of an integer.
Forgetting negative values of n in a general solution.
Including solutions outside a restricted interval.
Missing a solution because only one quadrant was considered.
Using a reference angle as though it were always the final angle.
Confusing a reference angle with the actual solution angle.
Mixing degrees and radians.
Leaving the calculator in the wrong angle mode.
Using decimal approximations when an exact unit-circle answer is available.
Forgetting that tangent is undefined at odd multiples of π/2.
Assuming a value outside the range of sine or cosine can still produce a real angle.
Using x = θ + 2nπ for tangent instead of x = θ + nπ.
Using only x = θ + 2nπ for sine equations of the form sin(x) = sin(θ) and missing the second family.
Using x = θ + 2nπ for cosine equations and missing the symmetric solution.
Forgetting that cos(x) = cos(θ) has the compact form x = 2nπ ± θ.
Forgetting that tan(x) = tan(θ) has the compact form x = θ + nπ.
Dividing by a trigonometric expression without considering whether it can equal zero.
Assuming that solving a transformed equation automatically guarantees every resulting value is valid.
Failing to check final answers against the original equation.
Forgetting that multiple-angle equations may produce more solutions within an interval because the angle expression changes faster.
